reason: The sources provide over 12 verified claims from at least two independent sites, including the dramatic details of the parachute failure, the discovery of the 'hidden' 23-minute signal, and the specific design challenges.
story: In 1970, the Soviet Union sent Venera 7 to the most hostile environment in the solar system: the surface of Venus. Built with a heavy titanium hull to withstand 180 atmospheres of pressure, the probe was a literal tank. However, during its final descent, the parachute failed, sending the lander into a 60 km/h freefall. It slammed into the Venusian soil and appeared to go silent. For weeks, scientists thought the surface mission was a failure. But radio astronomer Oleg Rzhiga refused to give up, painstakingly combing through the recording tapes. He discovered a miracle: a signal 100 times weaker than normal, buried in the background noise. The probe had survived the crash and landed on its side, pointing its antenna away from Earth. For 23 minutes, it whispered the first-ever data from the surface of another planet, confirming Venus was a 475-degree-Celsius furnace.
angle: The first data ever transmitted from another planet's surface was so faint it was only discovered weeks later, buried in background noise on a recording tape.

claims.claim: Venera 7 was a Soviet spacecraft launched on August 17, 1970.
Venera 7 was the first spacecraft to successfully transmit data from the surface of another planet.
The lander was constructed with a titanium hull to survive extreme pressure.
The probe was designed to withstand temperatures up to 540-580 degrees Celsius and pressures up to 180 atmospheres.
An internal switchboard failure during the mission caused the probe to only transmit temperature data.
The spacecraft was pre-cooled to -8 degrees Celsius before atmospheric entry to extend its lifespan.
The parachute failed or tore during the final descent, leading to a period of freefall.
Venera 7 impacted the surface of Venus at approximately 16.5 to 17 meters per second.
The lander touched down on the night side of Venus on December 15, 1970.
The probe landed on its side, causing the antenna to point away from Earth and weakening the signal.
Radio astronomer Oleg Rzhiga found 23 minutes of faint data buried in the recordings weeks after the landing.
The surface data confirmed a temperature of approximately 475 degrees Celsius.
The surface pressure was calculated to be approximately 90 atmospheres.
The rapid halt of the spacecraft indicated it hit a solid surface with low levels of dust.
Previous missions Venera 3 through 6 failed to return data from the Venusian surface.

disputed: The exact cause of the parachute failure (tearing versus melting reefing line) should be described as 'likely failure' or 'reconstructed' because no cameras were present.
The exact design temperature limit varies between 540°C and 580°C across sources; use a range or attribute as 'up to 580°C'.
